claims.text: The starting Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy is additively manufactured.
The starting alloy possesses a continuous FCC matrix.
The starting alloy's microstructure is optimized for strength and fatigue resistance.
High-temperature degradation of this alloy is governed by the quality of the surface oxide scale.
Oxidizing atmospheres rapidly produce a continuous, adherent Cr- and Al-enriched oxide layer on this alloy.
The continuous Cr- and Al-enriched oxide layer suppresses further oxidation.
Reducing or low-oxygen atmospheres prevent complete formation of the protective oxide scale.
Reducing conditions cause localized formation of less-adherent or volatile Ti-rich oxides.
The Ti-rich oxides compromise scale integrity and promote subsequent degradation.
Oxide-scale composition, continuity, and adherence mediate the relationship between gas atmosphere and degradation.
Oxidation kinetics are active over 700–1000 °C for the proposed alloy and atmospheres.
Under oxidizing conditions, the alloy will degrade more slowly than under reducing conditions.
Oxidizing exposure will produce minimal weight gain and better retention of mechanical properties.
Reducing exposure will cause abnormal weight loss or non-protective scale formation.
Reducing exposure will produce microstructural evidence of subsurface attack.
The as-manufactured baseline has no pre-existing oxide-scale artifacts.
The proposed mechanism applies between 700 and 1000 °C when the gas compositions clearly establish oxidizing or reducing conditions.
The central protective role of Cr- and Al-containing oxides is supported by analogous high-temperature-alloy studies.
Identical samples should be compared after fixed-duration oxidizing and reducing exposures at 700–1000 °C.

Failure to observe a more continuous Cr/Al-rich scale and better mechanical integrity in oxidizing conditions, or failure to associate Ti-rich oxides with degradation in reducing conditions, would falsify the hypothesis.
